exercises.title: AI Governance Communication
exercises.subtitle: Practise AI governance language: model registry, approval workflows, AI governance committees, and responsible deployment communication.

questions.q: A 'model registry' in an MLOps governance framework is used to:
options: Store user data for model training.
Centrally track approved model versions, their metadata, performance metrics, and deployment status.
Register models with a government authority.
List all open-source models available for use.
questions.explanation: A model registry (MLflow, SageMaker Model Registry) tracks model versions, evaluation results, approval status, and deployment history - providing auditability.

questions.q: An AI governance committee is responsible for:
options: Writing the code for AI models.
Reviewing proposed AI use cases for ethical, legal, and risk compliance before deployment approval.
Managing the cloud infrastructure that runs AI systems.
Setting the commercial pricing for AI products.
questions.explanation: AI governance committees (or ethics boards) review proposed AI applications against organisational policies, legal requirements, and ethical standards before approving deployment.

questions.q: In the context of AI deployment, 'human-in-the-loop' (HITL) means:
options: A human trains the model interactively.
A human reviews or approves AI decisions before they are acted upon.
The AI system cannot operate without a human pressing a button for each step.
Humans label all training data without any automation assistance.
questions.explanation: HITL keeps humans in the decision loop - the AI provides recommendations or flags cases, but a human validates before the decision is acted upon. Critical for high-stakes use cases.

questions.q: Which phrase best describes an AI system's 'kill switch' or 'human override'?
options: A physical power switch for the AI server.
A mechanism that allows authorised humans to halt or override the AI system's decisions or operation.
A monitoring alert that triggers when the model's accuracy drops.
A backup AI system that activates if the primary fails.
questions.explanation: The EU AI Act and AI safety frameworks require high-risk AI systems to include mechanisms for human override - allowing authorised personnel to stop or correct the system.

questions.q: What does 'model explainability' provide to stakeholders?
options: A technical description of how the neural network was trained.
An understandable explanation of why a specific AI decision was made, in terms the affected party can understand.
A report on the model's hardware utilisation.
A list of all training data used to build the model.
questions.explanation: Explainability enables affected people to understand AI decisions - required by GDPR (right to explanation) for automated decisions and by AI governance frameworks for high-risk use cases.

questions.q: PR Description During a code review of a new fraud detection model, Sarah notices the following comment from David: "This model uses a complex LSTM architecture. We need to ensure it's thoroughly tested for adversarial attacks - specifically, inputs designed to mislead the network. Consider adding more detailed documentation on the attack vectors we've considered and the mitigation strategies employed."
options: insufficient - the PR lacks clear metrics for model performance after testing.
adequate - the comment effectively highlights potential vulnerabilities and encourages further investigation.
overly cautious - the language suggests an unnecessary level of paranoia regarding LSTM models, potentially delaying deployment.
irrelevant - the comment focuses on a specific architectural detail (LSTM) rather than broader governance considerations.
questions.explanation: This is a good example of proactive governance communication within a code review. David's comment isn't simply pointing out a technical concern; he's specifically requesting documentation on attack vectors and mitigation strategies - crucial elements for demonstrating responsible AI development and meeting regulatory requirements. The incorrect options misinterpret the comment as insufficient or overly cautious, failing to recognize its value in establishing accountability and risk management around model deployment.

questions.q: During a standup update, Alex is explaining the deployment of their new AI-powered customer support chatbot. He mentions that 'we have a human-in-the-loop system' in place. Which of the following best describes what this means within the context of AI governance? Alex: 'We have a human-in-the-loop system.'
options: 'A team of customer service agents is continuously monitoring chatbot conversations for accuracy and escalating complex issues.'
'The chatbot automatically flags any conversation exceeding a certain length or containing ambiguous language, routing it to a human agent.'
'We've implemented a real-time feedback loop where human agents can correct the chatbot's responses directly within the system.'
'The chatbot only operates when there are no available human agents; otherwise, it is paused.'
questions.explanation: This question focuses on HITL implementation. Option A describes monitoring and escalation, not the core of a human-in-the-loop system. Option B details automated flagging but doesn't involve direct human intervention in correcting responses. Option C accurately represents the real-time feedback loop, allowing for continuous improvement and ensuring alignment with governance principles. Option D is an incorrect interpretation of paused operation.

questions.q: As a lead engineer, you're reviewing the PR description for a model that predicts loan defaults. The description states: 'The model incorporates feature selection to improve performance and reduce bias.' Which of the following is the MOST relevant governance consideration stemming from this statement? PR Description: 'The model incorporates feature selection to improve performance and reduce bias.'
options: 'We should prioritize minimizing the model's prediction latency, regardless of potential bias implications.'
'Detailed documentation of the feature selection process, including the rationale for removing specific features and any identified biases, is crucial.'
'The model's accuracy score alone provides sufficient evidence of its fairness and suitability for deployment.'
'We can ignore potential bias concerns as long as the model achieves a high overall accuracy rate.'
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding of bias mitigation. While performance is important, documentation of feature selection - especially regarding bias - is paramount. Option A prioritizes speed over governance. Option B directly addresses the need for transparency and accountability related to feature selection and bias. Options C and D represent flawed reasoning about model evaluation and risk acceptance, respectively.

exercises.title: AI Governance Frameworks Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practice vocabulary for AI governance: EU AI Act risk categories, NIST AI RMF, human review requirements, and AI audit language.

questions.q: Under the EU AI Act, a social scoring system used by a government is classified as ___ risk and is prohibited.
options: unacceptable - the highest risk tier; these systems are banned outright
high - regulated but permitted with strict requirements
limited - requires basic transparency obligations only
minimal - no specific obligations beyond existing law
questions.explanation: The EU AI Act's unacceptable risk category covers AI practices that pose a clear threat to fundamental rights - such as social scoring, real-time biometric surveillance in public spaces, and manipulation of vulnerable people. These are prohibited.

questions.q: A credit-scoring AI falls into the EU AI Act's ___ risk category. What does this require of the developer?
options: high - conformity assessment, risk management, data governance, and registration before deployment
unacceptable - the system must be discontinued immediately
limited - only a transparency notice to users
minimal - no additional obligations are imposed
questions.explanation: High-risk AI systems under the EU AI Act (e.g., credit scoring, hiring tools, critical infrastructure) must undergo conformity assessment, maintain technical documentation, implement risk management, and be registered in the EU database.

questions.q: Your team refers to the ___ AI RMF when designing your AI risk management process. What does this acronym stand for?
options: NIST - National Institute of Standards and Technology; their Risk Management Framework provides voluntary guidance
NATO - a defence alliance framework for AI in military contexts
NAIC - a US insurance regulatory framework
NBER - a research body that publishes AI economic impact reports
questions.explanation: The NIST AI RMF (AI Risk Management Framework) is a voluntary US framework that helps organizations identify, assess, and manage AI risks across four core functions: Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage.

questions.q: The compliance team confirms: 'This system requires a ___ review before any decision is finalised.' What safeguard is this?
options: human - a person must examine the AI output before it takes effect, preventing fully automated decisions
automated - the system reviews itself using a secondary model
legal - a lawyer must approve the output
technical - an engineer must re-run the model
questions.explanation: Human review (or human-in-the-loop) is a governance control that requires a person to examine and approve or override an AI decision before it becomes final - required for high-risk systems under frameworks like the EU AI Act.

questions.q: The governance office schedules an AI ___ to verify compliance with internal policies and external regulations.
options: audit - a systematic examination of the AI system's documentation, processes, and outputs for compliance
sprint - a development cycle focused on improving the AI model
benchmark - a performance test comparing the model to others
review - an informal peer check of the model's outputs
questions.explanation: An AI audit is a structured, formal examination of an AI system to verify it meets regulatory requirements, internal policies, and ethical standards - covering documentation, data practices, model behaviour, and incident logs.

questions.q: PR Description Subject: Refactor User Profile API - Enhanced Bias Detection During the code review of the new user profile API, lead developer Sarah flagged a potential issue. She suggested adding more granular controls to mitigate bias introduced during data enrichment, referencing discussions about 'explainable AI' and 'differential privacy' within the team's recent stand-up. She asked you to include a comment in the PR describing how you addressed this concern. Which of the following best reflects the kind of phrasing Sarah would expect to see in your comment?
options: Ensure all data enrichment processes adhere strictly to pre-defined rules, regardless of potential bias implications.
Implement differential privacy techniques to limit the information revealed during data enrichment and minimize the risk of unintended bias.
Document the specific steps taken to identify and mitigate potential biases in the data enrichment process, referencing relevant AI governance frameworks and explainable AI principles.
Leave the decision about bias mitigation to the compliance team; the API's functionality is fully compliant with existing regulations.
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding of applying AI governance vocabulary within a practical development scenario. Sarah's comment demonstrates an expectation beyond simply stating 'compliance.' She's asking for a description of *how* bias mitigation was addressed - specifically referencing techniques like differential privacy which are core to many modern AI governance frameworks. Option A is too rigid, option C emphasizes the crucial aspects of explainability and documentation that align with current best practices, and option D inappropriately delegates responsibility. The correct answer demonstrates awareness of technical approaches related to responsible AI development.

questions.q: Alex, a data scientist at 'Innovate Solutions,' is reviewing a PR for a new AI-powered customer support chatbot. The team has implemented differential privacy to minimize the risk of revealing sensitive user information. Sarah, the lead developer, comments: 'Great job incorporating differential privacy! Can you add more detail about how you're monitoring the system's output for potential biases?' Which phrasing best reflects what Sarah would expect in the PR comment?
questions.explanation: Sarah wants reassurance that the team is actively managing the risks associated with bias in the AI system. Simply stating they've used differential privacy isn't enough; she needs specifics on how it's being monitored and applied. This demonstrates a proactive approach to AI governance.

questions.q: Ben, a junior developer at 'QuantumLeap Tech,' is drafting the description for a PR introducing an automated risk assessment tool. The tool uses machine learning to predict potential regulatory violations based on company data. David, the compliance officer, asks Ben to clarify how they've addressed 'explainability' in the system's output. David wants to know if users can understand *why* the tool flagged a particular risk. Which of the following best describes the information Ben should include in the PR description?
questions.explanation: Explainability is crucial for regulatory compliance and building trust. Ben needs to outline how the tool's logic is translated into understandable terms, demonstrating accountability and allowing users to challenge findings. This aligns with the broader concept of AI governance frameworks.

questions.q: Chloe, a developer at 'Synergy Dynamics,' is reviewing a PR for an AI system designed to optimize supply chain logistics. The team has adopted an 'AI Risk Management Framework' (ARMF) during the development process. The governance office informs her that they require a formal 'Risk Assessment' as part of their ongoing monitoring. Which aspect of the ARMF does this statement primarily relate to?
questions.explanation: The ARMF emphasizes proactive risk management. The 'Risk Assessment' component is central to this framework - it's about systematically identifying potential harms (like supply chain disruptions or biased decisions) and developing strategies to address them before they occur. This directly supports the goals of AI governance.

exercises.title: AI Transparency Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practice AI transparency vocabulary: explainability reports, black box models, model documentation, flagging decisions for human review, and explaining model decisions.

questions.q: The compliance team requests an ___ report for the loan decision model. What does this document contain?
options: explainability - descriptions of which features drive predictions and how the model reaches its outputs
accuracy - precision and recall scores on the test set
latency - response time measurements for each prediction
deployment - infrastructure details for running the model in production
questions.explanation: An explainability report describes how a model makes decisions - which input features matter most, how they influence outputs, and how users or regulators can understand individual predictions. Required for high-risk AI systems.

questions.q: A regulator calls your model a '___ box model.' What are they criticising?
options: black - the model's internal reasoning is opaque and cannot be easily inspected or explained
white - the model is too transparent and leaks sensitive training data
grey - the model sometimes explains itself and sometimes does not
open - the model weights are publicly available
questions.explanation: A black box model is one whose internal workings are not interpretable - you can see the inputs and outputs but not the reasoning. Deep neural networks are often described this way, raising concerns for regulated domains.

questions.q: The team publishes ___ documentation covering the model's training data, intended use, and limitations.
options: model - a structured document (such as a model card) describing the system's purpose, data, performance, and constraints
API - technical reference for calling the model endpoint
infrastructure - server and deployment configuration details
test - results from the evaluation suite
questions.explanation: Model documentation (often a model card) is a standardised document that describes what a model does, what data it was trained on, its performance across subgroups, known limitations, and intended and prohibited uses.

questions.q: The system logs show: 'The decision was ___ for human review.' What happened?
options: flagged - the system identified uncertainty or a high-stakes case and queued it for a person to examine
approved - the model passed the decision to an automated executor
rejected - the model refused to make a prediction
archived - the decision was stored for future analysis
questions.explanation: When a decision is flagged for human review, the AI system has identified a case that exceeds a confidence threshold or matches a sensitivity rule, routing it to a human reviewer instead of acting automatically.

questions.q: In a stakeholder meeting you say: 'We can ___ 85% of decisions.' What are you communicating about the model?
options: explain - we can provide clear reasoning for 85% of outputs, though 15% remain opaque
predict - the model is correct 85% of the time
automate - 85% of cases require no human involvement
audit - we have logs covering 85% of historical decisions
questions.explanation: 'We can explain 85% of decisions' means that for 85% of model outputs, the system can provide an interpretable reason - such as the top contributing features - while the remaining 15% are still effectively a black box.

questions.q: Reviewer: 'I'm seeing a high degree of disagreement between the model's predictions and the actual outcomes in this fraud detection cohort. The explanations are also quite opaque - it's hard to understand *why* the model flagged these transactions as suspicious. PR Description: 'This PR implements the new fraud detection model, leveraging a gradient boosting algorithm for improved accuracy.' Which of the following best describes the reviewer's concern regarding this PR?
options: opaque - the model's decision-making process is not easily interpretable.
overfitting - the model performs exceptionally well on training data but poorly on unseen data.
biased - the model consistently favors one outcome over another due to skewed training data.
insufficient - the PR lacks adequate documentation regarding the model's limitations.
questions.explanation: The reviewer is highlighting a lack of transparency, specifically referring to 'opaque' decision-making. This term describes models where the reasoning behind predictions isn't clear or easily understood - often due to complex algorithms like gradient boosting. The options presented focus on different potential issues (overfitting, bias, insufficient documentation), but only 'opaque' directly addresses the core concern of difficult-to-interpret model behavior. It's crucial for developers to be able to articulate this lack of transparency when discussing models with stakeholders and reviewers.

questions.q: Reviewer: 'The model's output is consistently exhibiting bias across different demographic groups. While the technical documentation describes the training data preprocessing steps, it lacks a clear articulation of how potential biases were identified and mitigated - essentially, there's no transparency into the fairness evaluation process. PR Description: 'This PR updates the API endpoint to include confidence scores for each prediction.' Which phrase best captures the reviewer's primary concern?
options: Insufficient - the API documentation lacks technical detail.
Unexplained - the model demonstrates bias without mitigation strategies being documented.
Inaccurate - the confidence scores are misleading given the underlying bias.
Obsolete - the current API endpoint is no longer aligned with fairness requirements.
questions.explanation: The reviewer isn't primarily focused on the technical details of the API documentation (option A) or the accuracy of the confidence scores (option C). Instead, they are highlighting a critical lack of transparency regarding bias mitigation. The core issue is the absence of documented strategies for identifying and addressing potential biases within the model's training data and outputs - this directly relates to fairness concerns, which is why option B accurately reflects their concern. Option D is incorrect because the PR description itself focuses on API updates, not fairness evaluation.

questions.q: Senior Dev: 'Okay team, I've been reviewing the output from the new recommendation engine. The API response is returning these scores, but frankly, I don't understand *why* it's recommending this particular product to this user - there's no clear traceability back to their profile or past interactions. It feels like a black box! PR Description: 'This PR implements the new recommendation engine, utilizing collaborative filtering for personalized suggestions.' Which of the following best describes the issue highlighted by the Senior Dev?
options: opaque - the model lacks interpretability and clear justification for its recommendations.
robust - the API response consistently delivers high-quality product suggestions.
efficient - the algorithm quickly generates relevant recommendations without significant latency.
accurate - the scores align perfectly with user preferences based on historical data.
questions.explanation: The Senior Dev is concerned about the lack of transparency within the recommendation engine - a common problem when models are complex. Opaque refers to something that's difficult or impossible to understand, and in this context, it describes the model's decision-making process. The PR description focuses on implementation, not the crucial aspect of explainability, highlighting the need for a system where users can see *why* a recommendation was made.

questions.q: Reviewer: 'We've noticed a significant correlation between the model's output and certain protected characteristics - specifically, higher rates of denial for loan applications submitted by applicants from minority ethnic groups. While we've documented steps taken to address data bias during training, the model's decision-making process remains largely opaque. PR Description: 'This PR implements a new fairness metric and integrates it into the model evaluation pipeline.' Which phrase most accurately reflects the reviewer's concern?
options: insufficient - the model is not achieving acceptable accuracy rates.
opaque - the model's logic is difficult to understand, raising concerns about potential bias.
unvalidated - the current fairness metrics are inadequate for assessing discriminatory outcomes.
outdated - the documentation fails to reflect recent changes in the model's architecture.
questions.explanation: The reviewer is highlighting a critical issue: algorithmic bias. The core problem isn't simply about accuracy (option A), but about whether the model is producing *fair* outcomes across different demographic groups. 'Opaque' (option B) perfectly captures the concern that the decision-making process is not transparent, making it difficult to identify and correct potential biases-this is a key aspect of AI transparency. The PR focuses on metrics; the reviewer needs more than just measurement - they need insight into *why* the model is behaving in this way (option C). Simply updating metrics doesn't address the underlying lack of explainability (option D).

questions.q: During a Slack discussion about the new customer churn prediction model, Sarah writes: 'Just ran the explainability dashboard - it's showing that users flagged for potential churn are overwhelmingly associated with low engagement scores and infrequent logins. However, the *reason* why those low engagement scores are being predicted is… unclear. It just says 'model confidence.' This feels like we're building a system without understanding *why* it's making these decisions.' Which of the following best describes Sarah's concern?
options: Insufficient - the model doesn't provide any justification for its predictions.
Redundant - the explainability dashboard already clearly explains the reasons for churn prediction.
Unacceptable - the lack of transparency hinders our ability to debug and improve the model.

questions.q: In AI fairness, 'demographic parity' means a model should:
options: Be trained on equal numbers of samples from each demographic group.
Produce positive predictions at equal rates across demographic groups.
Use no demographic information as input features.
Be validated by representatives from each demographic group.
questions.explanation: Demographic parity (also called statistical parity) requires that the positive prediction rate is equal across groups - e.g., loan approval rates should be the same across racial groups.

questions.q: 'Disparate impact' in AI systems refers to:
options: A system that intentionally discriminates against a protected group.
When a facially neutral system disproportionately harms a protected group even without discriminatory intent.
The different performance of an AI system on different hardware.
When a system performs worse on rare classes in the training data.
questions.explanation: Disparate impact is a legal and ethical concept: a system can be discriminatory in effect (disparate impact) even if it was not designed to discriminate.

questions.q: What is 'selection bias' in a training dataset?
options: Deliberately selecting only accurate data for training.
When the training data is not representative of the real-world population the model will be applied to.
When the model selects only certain features during training.
The process of choosing which model architecture to use.
questions.explanation: Selection bias occurs when training data systematically misrepresents the deployment population - for example, a medical model trained on hospital records that over-represents severe cases.

questions.q: Equalized odds as a fairness metric requires that:
options: All groups have equal accuracy rates.
True positive rates and false positive rates are equal across protected groups.
The model is trained separately for each demographic group.
Positive predictions are equally distributed regardless of the actual label.
questions.explanation: Equalized odds requires both equal TPR (catching real positives) and equal FPR (avoiding false alarms) across groups - stricter than demographic parity alone.

questions.q: A 'red team' exercise in AI ethics involves:
options: A team of engineers who implement the model.
Adversarially probing a model to find harmful outputs, biases, or safety failures before deployment.
An external ethics board that approves AI use cases.
A group that manually labels data for the training set.
questions.explanation: AI red teaming involves actively trying to elicit harmful, biased, or unsafe outputs from a model to identify risks before deployment - borrowed from security red teaming.

questions.q: Reviewer: 'I've flagged this recommendation engine. The model consistently suggests higher interest rates to users identifying as 'Hispanic.' This feels… concerning. Can you investigate the data and feature engineering? (Excerpt from a Slack message during code review)
options: insufficient - the algorithm simply reflects existing lending disparities.
critical - this indicates potential algorithmic bias requiring immediate remediation and further analysis of the training data's representation.
neutral - it's acceptable for the model to correlate interest rates with demographic characteristics, as long as the overall loan approval rate remains equitable.
minor - a slight variation in recommendations is unavoidable given diverse user profiles; focus on optimizing prediction accuracy instead.
questions.explanation: This scenario highlights 'disparate impact,' which isn't merely about reflecting existing societal biases but rather when the algorithm *exacerbates* those biases. The reviewer correctly identifies a potentially harmful outcome - disproportionately higher interest rates for Hispanic users - and emphasizes the need for investigation and remediation. Simply accepting correlation as 'acceptable' ignores the ethical implications of algorithmic amplification.

questions.q: PR Description: 'Implemented new feature for fraud detection. Model now predicts higher risk scores for transactions originating from IP addresses in countries with historically high rates of fraudulent activity. Data was sourced primarily from publicly available government records.' What is the *primary* source of potential bias in this scenario?
options: A. The model's inherent complexity makes it difficult to interpret its decisions.
B. The selection bias introduced by using predominantly one data source - government records which may not accurately represent global transaction patterns.
C. The lack of human oversight during the model's training and deployment process.
D. The use of a standard machine learning library, which is known to be prone to errors.
questions.explanation: Selection bias occurs when the data used to train or evaluate a model isn't representative of the population it will eventually serve. In this case, relying solely on government records, likely skewed by reporting biases and geographic concentration, creates a biased training set. This leads to unfairly high risk scores for transactions originating from those countries, irrespective of individual user behavior. Options A and C are irrelevant to the core issue; option D is an unfounded criticism.

options: A. Algorithmic transparency - ensuring all model decisions are easily understandable.
B. Confirmation bias - the tendency to interpret new evidence as confirmation of existing beliefs.
C. Bias amplification - the phenomenon where a biased system's outputs exacerbate and reinforce initial biases.
D. Data drift - changes in the input data over time, leading to decreased model accuracy.
questions.explanation: Confirmation bias is closely related here; the chatbot's behavior is reinforcing pre-existing stereotypes by exhibiting different language styles based on gender identification. Minimal risk AI systems
High-risk AI systems
General-purpose AI models

questions.q: The EU AI Act 'conformity assessment' requires AI providers to:
options: Register their AI system with national authorities and pay a compliance fee.
Demonstrate their AI system meets the Act requirements before market placement.
Submit their AI model weights to the EU for review.
Obtain user consent before deploying any AI system.
questions.explanation: Conformity assessment is the process of demonstrating an AI system meets EU AI Act requirements - similar to CE marking for physical products.

questions.q: Which type of AI system is prohibited under the EU AI Act?
options: AI systems used for targeted advertising.
AI systems using subliminal techniques to manipulate behaviour in ways harmful to users.
AI systems that recommend content based on user preferences.
AI systems used for fraud detection in banking.
questions.explanation: The EU AI Act prohibits AI systems that use subliminal manipulation, exploit vulnerabilities, enable mass social scoring by governments, and certain biometric categorisation systems.

questions.q: An 'AI system card' or 'transparency obligation' for limited-risk AI requires:
options: Publishing the full training dataset.
Disclosing to users that they are interacting with an AI system when it is not obvious.
Conducting a full ethics review before deployment.
Registering with the EU AI Office annually.
questions.explanation: Limited-risk AI systems (chatbots, deepfakes) have transparency obligations - users must know when they are interacting with AI so they can make informed decisions.

questions.q: The EU AI Act defines GPAI (General Purpose AI) models as those that:

Are trained on large amounts of data and can be used for a wide range of tasks across many domains.

Run locally on user devices rather than in the cloud.

questions.q: The difference between model interpretability and model explainability is:
options: Interpretability means the model is accurate; explainability means it is fair.

An interpretable model is transparent by design (e.g. decision tree, linear regression) - its logic can be understood directly. Explainability refers to post-hoc methods that explain an opaque model's decisions after the fact.
Interpretability is for technical teams; explainability is for non-technical stakeholders.
They are synonyms - both mean the ability to understand why a model made a prediction.
questions.explanation: Interpretable models (logistic regression, decision trees) are intrinsically understandable. Black-box models (deep neural networks) require explainability techniques (SHAP, LIME) to provide post-hoc explanations of individual predictions.

questions.q: SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values tell you:
options: The overall accuracy of the model on the test set.
The contribution of each feature to a specific prediction - a positive SHAP value means the feature pushed the prediction higher; negative means it pushed it lower.
Whether the model satisfies demographic parity across groups.
How much the model's accuracy would change if you removed that feature entirely.
questions.explanation: SHAP values are grounded in Shapley values from game theory. Example: 'The age feature contributed +0.3 to the credit score prediction, while the high debt-to-income ratio contributed -0.8 - the primary reason for rejection.'

questions.q: LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) works by:
options: Training a simplified global model that approximates the complex model across all inputs.

Creating slightly modified versions of a specific input, running them through the model, and fitting a simple interpretable model (linear regression) to the local predictions - to explain a single prediction.
Visualising the gradient of the loss function with respect to input features.
Using attention weights to identify which input tokens the model focused on.
questions.explanation: LIME is local: it explains one prediction, not the whole model. It samples nearby inputs, observes the model's behaviour in that local neighbourhood, and fits a simple interpretable model to approximate the complex model's local decision boundary.

questions.q: A saliency map in computer vision explainability shows:
options: The geographic regions where the training data was collected.
Which pixels or image regions had the most influence on the model's prediction - typically shown as a heatmap overlaid on the image.
The locations in the dataset most similar to the input image.
A map of the model's confidence score across different image categories.
questions.explanation: Saliency maps (and related Grad-CAM, gradient-weighted class activation maps) highlight what the model 'looked at' when making its decision. Example: a diagnostic AI highlighting the tumour region that drove its classification.

questions.q: When communicating an AI explanation to a non-technical stakeholder, the best approach is:
options: Show the full SHAP waterfall plot and explain Shapley value mathematics.

Translate the technical explanation into business-relevant terms: 'The main reason the loan was declined was the high debt-to-income ratio and the short credit history - not the applicant's age or location.'
Avoid explaining the AI decision to prevent the stakeholder from challenging it.
Always qualify the explanation as unreliable since AI decisions cannot be truly explained.
questions.explanation: Effective AI explanations for non-technical audiences use natural language, concrete examples, and avoid statistical jargon. They should answer the specific question the stakeholder cares about ('why was this decision made?') rather than explaining the method.

exercises.title: Human-in-the-Loop Language
exercises.subtitle: Practise vocabulary for HITL, HOTL, automation levels, human oversight, and override communication in AI systems.

questions.q: Human-in-the-loop (HITL) means:
options: An AI system that learns from human users as they interact with it.
A system design where a human actively participates in each decision cycle - reviewing AI outputs and approving or rejecting them before they take effect.
Using human feedback to retrain the AI model after deployment.
A support process where humans handle queries the AI cannot answer.
questions.explanation: HITL is the strictest oversight model: the AI suggests, the human approves. Used in high-stakes domains (medical diagnosis approval, legal document review, loan underwriting). The human is in the decision loop, not just monitoring.

questions.q: Human-on-the-loop (HOTL) is best described as:
options: A human who monitors AI decisions in real time and can intervene when needed, but does not actively approve each decision before it takes effect.
A training approach where humans label data that is immediately used to retrain the model.
A human who reviews all AI decisions retrospectively after they have been made.
An escalation path activated only when the AI produces an error.
questions.explanation: HOTL: the AI acts autonomously, but a human monitors and can override. Used in autonomous vehicle monitoring, automated trading oversight, content moderation review queues. Lower friction than HITL but less strict oversight.

questions.q: The phrase 'if the confidence score falls below 0.7, the decision is escalated to a human agent' describes:
options: A human-in-the-loop system where all decisions require human approval.
A human-on-the-loop design where the AI acts autonomously for high-confidence decisions and escalates uncertain cases to human review.
A human-out-of-the-loop system with an emergency fallback.
A model calibration process to improve confidence score accuracy.
questions.explanation: Confidence-based escalation is a common HOTL pattern: the AI handles most cases autonomously (efficiency) but routes uncertain cases to humans (safety). The threshold (0.7) defines the automation/human boundary.

questions.q: Audit trail requirements for AI-assisted human decisions mean:
options: The AI must be audited annually by an independent third party.
Both the AI's recommendation and the human's final decision must be logged - enabling review of whether humans are appropriately overriding AI suggestions or rubber-stamping them.
A trail of breadcrumbs that allows the user to navigate back through AI decisions.
The requirement to log all model training runs for regulatory review.
questions.explanation: Audit trails for HITL/HOTL systems are essential for accountability: logging the AI output, human decision, timestamp, and operator ID allows regulators and quality teams to verify that human oversight is genuinely occurring - not just nominal.

questions.q: The correct term for the scenario where 'a human reviewer must approve all outputs in the high-risk category before they are sent to the customer' is:
options: Human-out-of-the-loop with high-risk exceptions.
Human-in-the-loop - a human is required to approve each high-risk decision before it takes effect.
Human-on-the-loop - the human monitors the stream of decisions.
Full automation with human escalation on error.
questions.explanation: Requiring approval before the decision takes effect = HITL. 'The output is held until a human reviews it' is the defining HITL characteristic - distinguishing it from HOTL where the decision can execute before the human reviews it.

exercises.title: AI Model Audit Language
exercises.subtitle: Practise vocabulary for red-teaming, robustness testing, audit findings, and writing AI model assessments.

questions.q: AI red-teaming is defined as:
options: A competitive exercise where two teams of data scientists build rival models.
Adversarial testing conducted to proactively discover failure modes, harmful outputs, safety gaps, and edge cases in an AI system before deployment.
A security penetration test focused exclusively on the model's training data.
The process of reviewing a model's source code for security vulnerabilities.
questions.explanation: AI red-teaming (distinct from security red-teaming) focuses on eliciting undesirable model behaviours: harmful content generation, bias amplification, safety bypass, jailbreaking, and factual errors. It is a structured adversarial evaluation, not a code review.

questions.q: Out-of-distribution (OOD) detection in model robustness refers to:
options: Detecting inputs that fall outside the model's confidence threshold.
Identifying when an input is significantly different from the training data distribution - inputs the model has not seen and on which its predictions may be unreliable.
Distributing the model's load across multiple servers to handle edge cases.
Detecting distribution of model outputs that are outside business acceptable ranges.
questions.explanation: OOD detection is critical for safe deployment: a model trained on US medical records may perform poorly on data from a different healthcare system. Flagging OOD inputs allows the system to route uncertain cases to human review instead of auto-deciding.

questions.q: When writing an AI audit finding, the standard structure includes:
options: Only the issue description - the team can determine the impact themselves.
The observation (what was found), the evidence (how it was discovered), the risk or impact (what could go wrong), and the recommendation (what to do about it).
A list of all red-team prompts used during the assessment.
The academic papers that support the existence of this type of AI failure.
questions.explanation: Structured audit findings enable efficient remediation: Observation: 'The model responds to [specific prompt category] with harmful content.' Evidence: '[Example inputs and outputs].' Risk: 'Violates content policy; potential legal liability.' Recommendation: 'Add output-layer content filter for [category].'

questions.q: Covariate shift means a model may underperform when:
options: The model is deployed on different hardware than it was trained on.
The distribution of input features in production differs from the training distribution - the real-world data looks different from what the model learned on.
The model's target variable definition changes between training and deployment.
Multiple models are trained simultaneously on different feature subsets.
questions.explanation: Covariate shift is common when training data is not representative of production. Example: a fraud detection model trained on 2021 transactions may underperform in 2024 because spending patterns have changed - the input feature distribution has shifted.

questions.q: Third-party AI audit vocabulary includes 'attestation', which means:
options: The third-party auditor's billing for the audit engagement.
A formal written declaration by the auditor confirming that the AI system meets specified requirements or standards based on the evidence reviewed.
The process of adding additional test cases to an audit framework.
A document listing all the data used to train the model under review.
questions.explanation: Attestation is a formal audit output: the auditor 'attests' (formally declares) that the system satisfies the stated criteria. It is stronger than an informal assessment and provides a basis for regulatory compliance claims.

exercises.title: Responsible AI Development Vocabulary
exercises.subtitle: Practice vocabulary for responsible AI development: responsible AI principles, fairness-aware ML, demographic parity, model performance on minority classes, and testing for bias.

questions.q: Your organization publishes a set of ___ AI principles covering fairness, transparency, and accountability.
options: responsible - a framework guiding ethical AI design and deployment
generative - principles specifically for large language models
open - principles that make all model weights publicly available
adaptive - principles that change as the model learns
questions.explanation: Responsible AI principles are an organization's stated commitments to building and deploying AI ethically - typically covering fairness, reliability, safety, privacy, inclusivity, transparency, and accountability.

questions.q: The ML team adopts ___-aware ML to ensure the model does not disadvantage any group.
options: fairness - training and evaluating with explicit attention to equitable outcomes across groups
cost - optimising the model to minimise inference expense
speed - prioritising low-latency predictions
accuracy - maximising overall correct predictions regardless of group
questions.explanation: Fairness-aware ML integrates fairness constraints and metrics into the model development process - choosing algorithms, loss functions, and evaluation criteria that reduce discriminatory outcomes.

questions.q: An audit reveals the model violates ___ parity: approval rates differ significantly by protected group.
options: demographic - a fairness metric requiring equal outcome rates across demographic groups
numeric - a technical metric about precision and recall
statistical - a general term for any measurable discrepancy
temporal - a metric comparing model performance over time
questions.explanation: Demographic parity (also called statistical parity) requires that the proportion of positive predictions is equal across demographic groups. Violating it means the model favours or disadvantages certain groups.

questions.q: The evaluation report notes: 'The model performs worse on ___ classes.' What does this mean?
options: minority - groups that are underrepresented in the training data, leading to lower accuracy for them
outlier - data points far from the mean that skew results
majority - groups that dominate the training set
synthetic - artificially generated training examples
questions.explanation: When a model performs worse on minority classes, it means that underrepresented groups in the training data receive less accurate predictions - a common fairness problem caused by imbalanced datasets.

questions.q: Before launch the team runs a suite of tests ___ for bias to verify fairness across subgroups.
options: testing for bias - systematically evaluating whether the model disadvantages protected groups
screening for accuracy - measuring overall prediction correctness
checking for latency - measuring inference speed
auditing for cost - calculating the expense of running the model
questions.explanation: Testing for bias involves running targeted evaluations that compare model performance across protected attributes (gender, ethnicity, age, etc.) to identify and quantify unfair outcomes before deployment.

questions.q: PR Description Subject: Refactor User Profile API - Added Deprecation Warnings Body: Hi team, This PR introduces deprecation warnings for the legacy user profile endpoint ( /v1/users/{user_id} ). We're transitioning to a new, more efficient API and want to give users time to migrate. I've included logging around these warnings to help us monitor usage. Please review and let me know if you have any concerns about the impact on existing integrations. Thanks, John
options: Implement robust error handling to prevent unexpected API failures.
Prioritize performance optimization by reducing database queries.
Ensure clear documentation of the deprecation process and migration path, acknowledging potential disruption for dependent services - particularly regarding logging as a key monitoring metric.
Immediately remove the legacy endpoint to enforce the new API standard.
questions.explanation: This question assesses understanding of communicating responsible AI changes within a development workflow. The correct answer emphasizes documentation and acknowledging potential disruption - a crucial aspect of mitigating risks associated with transitioning APIs. Options A and B focus on technical aspects that are important but miss the core concern about user impact and dependency management. Option D is overly aggressive and ignores best practices for phased rollouts.

questions.q: During a code review discussion about the user profile API changes, Sarah asks: 'John, are we considering potential downstream effects of these deprecation warnings? Specifically, what measures have we taken to ensure that older integrations relying on this endpoint don't experience unexpected errors or data inconsistencies when they eventually receive the warning messages?'
options: 'We've simply added logging; the clients will handle the transition.'
'We've proactively tested all known legacy integrations and confirmed compatibility with the new API.'
'We're implementing robust error handling and monitoring to catch any unexpected issues arising from the deprecation warnings, along with clear documentation for migrating users.'
'The warning messages are designed to be subtle, so clients shouldn't notice anything.'
questions.explanation: This question assesses understanding of responsible AI beyond just adding logging. While logging is a step, it doesn't address the potential for integration failures or data inconsistencies when older systems receive deprecation warnings. Option 2 correctly highlights proactive testing and comprehensive error handling - crucial components of mitigating risk in a phased API transition. Options A, C, and D all represent insufficient consideration of downstream impacts and user experience during a change like this; they demonstrate a lack of awareness regarding integration dependencies and potential disruption.

questions.q: Mark from the data science team sends this message: 'Just ran a quick fairness check on the loan application model - saw a significant disparity in approval rates for applicants with addresses in historically redlined neighborhoods. Need to investigate further.' What does Mark likely mean when he mentions 'fairness check'?
options: He is verifying that the model uses only neutral language.
He is assessing whether the model's predictions are biased against certain demographic groups based on their location.
He is confirming that the model adheres strictly to all legal regulations regarding lending practices.
He is ensuring the model generates accurate risk scores for each applicant.
questions.explanation: Mark uses 'fairness check' to indicate he's examining whether the model produces different outcomes (like approval rates) for groups based on sensitive attributes (in this case, location). This is a core concept in responsible AI - ensuring equitable results regardless of group membership. The other options relate to legal compliance or risk scoring, but don't address the fundamental issue of bias.

questions.q: During a code review, David comments on this snippet: ```python def predict_fraud(user_data): # Uses features like age and income to score risk. return model.predict(user_data) ``` What is David most likely concerned about regarding the use of 'age' and 'income' as features?
options: The code doesn't handle missing data effectively.
The model might be unfairly discriminating against younger or lower-income individuals due to historical biases in those groups.
The code lacks proper documentation for the model itself.
The model is using a complex algorithm that's difficult to understand.
questions.explanation: David's concern centers on 'fairness' - age and income are frequently correlated with protected characteristics (like race or gender). If the model relies heavily on these features without addressing potential bias, it could perpetuate discriminatory outcomes. It is a critical consideration when building AI systems.
